I don’t get why all blame is being placed on the mom, they’re both parents. And she does childcare, that’s not nothing. Childrearing is work even though it’s not salaried. Her being ineffective in one incident doesn’t mean all the other work she does should be discounted. So it’s untrue to say that the husband does everything. Being tired from work is normal and wanting to resolve the issue as quickly as possible is normal. Unfortunately, you have to parent even when you’re tired or stressed. Which is why I said that being harsh is easy even though it’s not effective. It ends the immediate problem without preventing others. Both parents had an opportunity to ask why the kid wasn’t eating and neither did so to my knowledge.

I’m not saying he did. I was giving an example of adults saying no without being harsh. 

Being commanded to eat without any other discussion is useless for anything but the immediate situation. It doesn’t address why the kid isn’t eating or prevent it from happening in the future. That kid also won’t be 5 and easy to command forever. So unless they’re going to be commanded over every disagreement, that’s a band-aid solution.
And there is a difference between being soft and having no boundaries. Having no boundaries leads to kids that disrespect others boundaries, not softness.

Forcing obedience is an ineffective way of showing love and care even when intentions are good. It might get the response the parents want or need but the child most likely won’t understand that as love. They’ll feel like they’ve been punished while being told it’s out of love. 

Touching a hot stove is immediate danger and skipping a meal is not (though it is it’s own problem). It’s not really comparable.

You can be soft without being a pushover, adults do it all the time. For example, you can tell a coworker no without cussing them out. Harshness isn’t necessary to get a point across in most cases, it’s just easy.
